A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPARKLING study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original MoE training experiments, downstream evaluations, computational measurements, and ablations in Sections 3-5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, prior-method comparisons, dense-model experiments, iterative expansion, and compute-matched analyses.

M1.justification: Both versions use RMS-preserving rescaling, copy initialization, asymmetric optimizer-state reset, and asymmetric learning-rate re-warmup. v2 applies the same components to dense models and successive expansions. Its explicit RMSNorm initialization default clarifies implementation rather than establishing an algorithm change.

E1.justification: The language-modeling task and the 12 downstream evaluation columns remain unchanged; v2's Tables 6-8 reuse the evaluations in Table 1. No new corpus, language, or domain is reported. Dense architectures, successive expansions, and compute matching change configurations and procedures within the retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix K and Table 7 add evaluated dynamics-based comparators: Scaled Opt. + Remap LR, Uneven Splitting with 25%/50% Faster Decay LR, and FP-random + WN-Adapted LR. Table 7 also introduces downstream comparisons with previously loss-only heuristic baselines. Table 1's renamed Naive FP scaled baseline retains its original numerical results.

E3.justification: The original single expansion at 100B of 200B tokens is retained. v2 adds a dense configuration with intermediate size 4096 and a two-stage 256-to-512-to-1024 expansion at 50B and 100B tokens (Appendices N-O). Appendix P introduces comparisons at equal-FLOP points on training trajectories, substantially extending the original fixed-token evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled RMSNorm copy-versus-random ablation (Appendix C), a four-configuration separation of RMS preservation and asymmetric strategies across three initialization pairs (Appendix I), and an analysis of immediate perturbation versus final loss (Appendix F). Iterative and compute-matched analyses further examine efficiency and composability. The original Muon tests and re-warmup sensitivity analysis are retained after relocation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a statistical uncertainty-estimation procedure. The added results continue the existing point-estimate and training-curve reporting practice.

E6.justification: The numerical results in Tables 1 and 2 remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial ablation and comparator results in Tables 6-7, dense results in Table 8, and iterative and compute-matched findings. Table 8 reports downstream averages of 53.78 for SPARKLING, 53.39 for training from scratch, and 52.00 for naive expansion. Figure 14 reports a 0.0306 dense-model loss advantage at matched compute. These are additional comparisons, not improvements over v1 under changed settings.

T1.justification: The RMS-preservation derivations, gradient-symmetry analysis, optimizer argument, scheduling equations, and Appendix A assumptions and derivations are mathematically retained. The added post-normalization, scaling, and iterative-expansion discussions provide qualitative arguments rather than new formal proofs or substantive revisions to the existing mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list broaden the empirical generality claim from MoE models to dense and MoE architectures; the conclusion also includes multiple expansion stages. The central signal-preservation/symmetry-breaking contribution and the headline claim of up to 35% computational savings remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting the residual training-loss gap to reduced compute and downstream generalization to loss-landscape geometry (Section 5.1). It interprets compute-matched gains as a larger scaling exponent (Section 5.5 and Appendix P), extends the RMS argument to post-normalization, and discusses iterative expansion's loss/compute tradeoff and further-stage limitations. These substantially extend v1's interpretation, although the claimed exponent improvement lacks a fitted scaling analysis.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents copy initialization for RMSNorm weights and supplies implementation recipes for the added dynamics baselines, including schedule remapping and accelerated decay. It also specifies the dense and iterative configurations. The original architecture, training hyperparameters, and hardware information in Tables 3-5 are retained, with the setup appendix moved from B to D.

R1.justification: The distinct cited works are retained after matching publication updates and the consolidated OLMoE references. Sections 5.2 and Appendices K-L extend the positioning through explicit superiority claims over the dynamics-based approaches of Shen et al., Wang et al., and Yuan et al., previously discussed without these direct comparisons.

P1.justification: The six main sections and much of the original prose remain intact. v2 makes local language and terminology corrections, clarifies baseline names and defaults, expands Section 5 into five subsections, and reorganizes the appendices. Author information, citation style, acknowledgements, and an impact statement also change.

P2.justification: The single-column branded report becomes a two-column conference-format main text with different typography, headers, captions, and float placement. Retained figures are restyled or relocated, and configuration tables are arranged side by side. Three new tables and seven new figures display the added ablations, comparisons, and scaling analyses.

improvement.justification: The new component ablation and evaluated dynamics-based comparators address important gaps in evidence for combining RMS preservation with asymmetric optimization. Dense and iterative experiments strengthen applicability, while matched-FLOP comparisons complement v1's fixed-token efficiency argument. Together these substantially improve support for the central contribution. The new scaling-exponent interpretation exceeds what the plotted comparisons establish, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger controlled empirical evidence.
